title: Listening in Devgandhari
hookLine: a short hymn sounds bleak the first time; the second time, you hear where it ends

cards: A text message arrives: we need to talk. Read it once, fast, and it can sound like trouble. Read it again, slowly, and you notice the little smile at the end.
Same words, different message. Speed changes what you hear, and short pieces are the easiest to rush, because they're over before you've arrived.
Devgandhari is a short section of the Granth, and today's hymn from it is short too. Both reward the opposite of rushing.

teach.b: Take one of Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns in Devgandhari. Hear it once, quickly, and here's roughly what lands, in plain English: in this world I have seen that love is false.
Everyone is attached to their own comfort, whether spouse or friend.

teach.h: MINE, MINE, AND NO ONE GOES ALONG.
teach.b: Everyone says mine, mine, and binds the heart to self-interest. At the end, no one goes along. It sounds bleak, and a first listen might stop right there and file it under gloomy.
Now hear it again, slowly. The hymn speaks to the foolish mind that still doesn't understand, though the Guru keeps teaching it: yesterday's gentleness, the patient voice.
And then the last line, the one a rushed ear misses: Nanak says the one who sings the songs of God crosses the fearful ocean. The hymn doesn't end in the dark.
It ends on singing, which is exactly what the listener is hearing at that moment.
Heard slowly, a short hymn that seemed a single mood has a shape: a hard look at things, a patient word to the mind, and a turn toward the Name.
The Guru set it in a gentle raga, so even the hard opening is sung softly, and the singing carries you to the end.
So listen twice: the first time, let the words go by; the second time, slowly, listen for where the hymn ends up.

how: In kirtan, ragis return to a shabad's refrain line between verses, so the listener hears its center again and again; Guru Tegh Bahadur's Devgandhari hymns are sung in that gentle raga.

s: Guru Tegh Bahadur's Devgandhari hymn ends in despair
it ends with Nanak saying the one who sings God's songs crosses the fearful ocean.
a short hymn can have a turn that a quick listen misses
this one moves from a hard look at the world to the singing that carries across.

games.q: you've heard a short hymn once, and it sounded bleak. what do you do?
o: skip it; you've got the gist.
listen again, slowly, for where it ends.
games.why: a second, slower listen reaches the last line: the one who sings the songs of God crosses the fearful ocean. the hymn ends on singing.

practice: Bring back one sentence from today, everyone says mine, mine, or the one who sings crosses over, and say it once in your head at normal speed.

Then say it again, half as fast, letting each word land before the next one starts, and notice which word gets heavier the second time. Stay with that word, and if you pray, let it lead into Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Listening in Devgandhari. Short hymns heard twice, slowly, so the turn at the end isn't missed. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: twice, slowly. The hymn's turn waits in its last line. Back tomorrow, same hill.
